claim: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen that resides in a membrane-bound compartment, the inclusion.
source: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen that resides in a membrane-bound compartment, the inclusion.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about C. trachomatis biology presented in the abstract.

claim: Chlamydia bacteria secrete a unique class of proteins, Incs, which insert into the inclusion membrane and modulate the host-bacterium interface.
source: The bacteria secrete a unique class of proteins, Incs, which insert into the inclusion membrane and modulate the host-bacterium interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Inc proteins cited in the abstract.

claim: IncE binds specifically to the Sorting Nexin 5 Phox domain (SNX5-PX).
source: We previously reported that IncE binds specifically to the Sorting Nexin 5 Phox domain (SNX5-PX) and disrupts retromer trafficking.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work by the authors and is confirmed by the crystal structure presented in this manuscript.

claim: IncE disrupts retromer trafficking.
source: We previously reported that IncE binds specifically to the Sorting Nexin 5 Phox domain (SNX5-PX) and disrupts retromer trafficking.
evidence: This is supported by previous work and the current study's findings on CI-MPR trafficking.

claim: The crystal structure of the SNX5-PX:IncE complex shows IncE bound to a unique and highly conserved hydrophobic groove on SNX5.
source: Here, we present the crystal structure of the SNX5-PX:IncE complex, showing IncE bound to a unique and highly conserved hydrophobic groove on SNX5.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in Figure 1 and the structural analysis.

claim: Mutagenesis of the SNX5-PX:IncE binding surface disrupts a previously unsuspected interaction between SNX5 and the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR).
source: Mutagenesis of the SNX5-PX:IncE binding surface disrupts a previously unsuspected interaction between SNX5 and the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR).
evidence: This is supported by the AP-MS data showing loss of CI-MPR binding to SNX5 mutants.

claim: Addition of IncE peptide inhibits the interaction of CI-MPR with SNX5.
source: Addition of IncE peptide inhibits the interaction of CI-MPR with SNX5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peptide competition assay shown in Figure 4.

claim: C. trachomatis infection interferes with the SNX5:CI-MPR interaction.
source: Finally, C. trachomatis infection interferes with the SNX5:CI-MPR interaction, suggesting that IncE and CI-MPR are dependent on the same binding surface on SNX5.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments during infection shown in Figure 5.

claim: IncE and CI-MPR are dependent on the same binding surface on SNX5.
source: Finally, C. trachomatis infection interferes with the SNX5:CI-MPR interaction, suggesting that IncE and CI-MPR are dependent on the same binding surface on SNX5.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis, peptide competition, and infection experiments.

claim: C. trachomatis infection is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted disease.
source: C. trachomatis infection is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted disease and a leading cause of preventable infertility in the western world.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: C. trachomatis infection is a leading cause of preventable infertility in the western world.
source: C. trachomatis infection is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted disease and a leading cause of preventable infertility in the western world.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Infections by C. trachomatis lead to blinding trachoma, the major cause of non-congenital blindness in developing nations.
source: Infections by C. trachomatis also lead to blinding trachoma, the major cause of non-congenital blindness in developing nations.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: A successful vaccine for C. trachomatis remains elusive.
source: Understanding the pathogenesis of C. trachomatis infections is critical to the development of a successful vaccine, which remains elusive (Rey-Ladino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rey-Ladino et al., 2014.

claim: All Chlamydia species share a common intracellular developmental cycle in which they alternate between an infectious, spore-like elementary body (EB), and a non-infectious, metabolically active reticulate body (RB).
source: All Chlamydia species share a common intracellular developmental cycle in which they alternate between an infectious, spore-like elementary body (EB), and a non-infectious, metabolically active reticulate body (RB) (Bastidas et al., 2013; Elwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydia biology supported by citations.

claim: Upon entry into non-phagocytic cells, the EB resides within a membrane-bound compartment—the inclusion—and quickly diverges from the canonical endo-lysosomal pathway.
source: Upon entry into non-phagocytic cells, the EB resides within a membrane-bound compartment—the inclusion—and quickly diverges from the canonical endo-lysosomal pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydia infection.

claim: The EB differentiates into an RB and bacterial cell division commences.
source: The EB differentiates into an RB and bacterial cell division commences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Chlamydia developmental cycle.

claim: After replicating within the ever-enlarging inclusion over a 24–72 hr time period, the RB differentiates back to an EB.
source: After replicating within the ever-enlarging inclusion over a 24–72 hr time period, the RB differentiates back to an EB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Chlamydia developmental cycle.

claim: Mature EBs are released by host cell lysis or through an active extrusion process.
source: Mature EBs are released by host cell lysis or through an active extrusion process, ready to infect neighboring cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Chlamydia release mechanisms.

claim: Chlamydiae are absolutely reliant on altering host cell trafficking to scavenge nutrients while avoiding lysosomal fusion and recognition by the host innate immune system.
source: As obligate intracellular pathogens, Chlamydiae are absolutely reliant on altering host cell trafficking to scavenge nutrients while avoiding lysosomal fusion and recognition by the host innate immune system (Bastidas et al., 2013; Elwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Chlamydia inclusion maintains an intimate interaction with multiple host cell compartments and organelles, including the Golgi, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), mitochondria, endosomes, and lipid droplets.
source: The Chlamydia inclusion maintains an intimate interaction with multiple host cell compartments and organelles, including the Golgi, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), mitochondria, endosomes, and lipid droplets (Bastidas et al., 2013; Elwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Chlamydia factors and host cell proteins that mediate interactions between the inclusion and host organelles are largely unknown.
source: However, the Chlamydia factors and host cell proteins that mediate these interactions are largely unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Inclusion membrane proteins (Incs) are a group of proteins that are unique to Chlamydiales and that are translocated from the bacteria through the Type III secretion system (T3SS) and inserted into the inclusion membrane.
source: Likely bacterial candidates include the inclusion membrane proteins (Incs), a group of proteins that are unique to Chlamydiales and that are translocated from the bacteria through the Type III secretion system (T3SS) and inserted into the inclusion membrane (Moore and Ouellette, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Inc proteins supported by citation.

claim: Incs encode one or more bilobed hydrophobic domains composed of two closely spaced membrane-spanning domains, ~30 amino acids each, typically separated by a short loop region.
source: These proteins encode one or more bilobed hydrophobic domains composed of two closely spaced membrane-spanning domains, ~30 amino acids each, typically separated by a short loop region (Bannantine et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Inc proteins supported by citation.

claim: Once inserted into the inclusion membrane, the Inc N- and C-terminal domains extend into the host cytoplasm.
source: Once inserted into the inclusion membrane, the Inc N- and C-terminal domains extend into the host cytoplasm (Rockey et al., 2002) and are thus ideally poised to modulate interactions at the host-pathogen interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Inc N- and C-terminal domains are ideally poised to modulate interactions at the host-pathogen interface.
source: Once inserted into the inclusion membrane, the Inc N- and C-terminal domains extend into the host cytoplasm (Rockey et al., 2002) and are thus ideally poised to modulate interactions at the host-pathogen interface.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the topology of Inc proteins.

claim: Until recently, the host targets of only a few Incs had been identified.
source: Until recently, the host targets of only a few Incs had been identified (Elwell et al., 2016; Moore and Ouellette, 2014).
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: High-throughput affinity purification-mass spectrometry (AP-MS) was used to globally define the Inc-human protein interactome and identified putative binding partners for 38/58 of the C. trachomatis Incs.
source: We used high-throughput affinity purification-mass spectrometry (AP-MS) to globally define the Inc-human protein interactome and identified putative binding partners for 38/58 of the C. trachomatis Incs (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by previous work by the authors cited.

claim: One of the most robust interactions was between IncE, an early expressed Inc, and a subset of retromer components.
source: One of the most robust interactions was between IncE, an early expressed Inc (Scidmore-Carlson et al., 1999), and a subset of retromer components.
evidence: This is supported by previous AP-MS data and the citation about IncE expression timing.

claim: IncE is an early expressed Inc.
source: One of the most robust interactions was between IncE, an early expressed Inc (Scidmore-Carlson et al., 1999), and a subset of retromer components.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scidmore-Carlson et al., 1999.

claim: The retromer is a phylogenetically conserved multi-subunit complex that mediates retrograde transport of transmembrane protein cargo from endosomes to the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: The retromer is a phylogenetically conserved multi-subunit complex that mediates retrograde transport of transmembrane protein cargo, such as the well-studied cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR), from endosomes to the trans-Golgi network (TGN) (reviewed in [Liu, 2016]).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retromer function supported by citation.

claim: CI-MPR is a well-studied cargo of the retromer.
source: The retromer is a phylogenetically conserved multi-subunit complex that mediates retrograde transport of transmembrane protein cargo, such as the well-studied cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-MPR), from endosomes to the trans-Golgi network (TGN) (reviewed in [Liu, 2016]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Retromer is composed of two distinct sub-complexes of tightly assembled subunits: a cargo recognition trimer (VPS26/29/35) and a membrane deforming heterodimer made up of sorting nexin (SNX) SNX1 or SNX2 paired with either SNX5 or SNX6.
source: Retromer is composed of two distinct sub-complexes of tightly assembled subunits: a cargo recognition trimer (VPS26/29/35) and a membrane deforming heterodimer made up of sorting nexin (SNX) SNX1 or SNX2 paired with either SNX5 or SNX6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retromer structure.

claim: In mammals, as opposed to yeast, the association between the VPS trimer and the SNX sub-complexes is transient.
source: In mammals, as opposed to yeast, the association between the VPS trimer and the SNX sub-complexes is transient.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian retromer assembly.

claim: The individual SNX1/2/5/6 proteins encode a Phox-homology (PX) domain that recognizes and binds to specific phosphoinositides on membranes.
source: The individual SNX1/2/5/6 proteins encode a Phox-homology (PX) domain that recognizes and binds to specific phosphoinositides on membranes and a Bin-amphiphysin-Rvs (BAR) domain that both senses and induces membrane curvature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNX protein domains.

claim: The individual SNX1/2/5/6 proteins encode a Bin-amphiphysin-Rvs (BAR) domain that both senses and induces membrane curvature.
source: The individual SNX1/2/5/6 proteins encode a Phox-homology (PX) domain that recognizes and binds to specific phosphoinositides on membranes and a Bin-amphiphysin-Rvs (BAR) domain that both senses and induces membrane curvature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNX protein domains.

claim: SNX-BAR proteins facilitate formation of tubules into which the cargo receptors are sorted.
source: These SNX-BAR proteins facilitate formation of tubules into which the cargo receptors are sorted.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNX-BAR protein function.

claim: C. trachomatis IncE binds directly to the PX domains of SNX5/6 but not SNX1/2.
source: We recently discovered that C. trachomatis IncE binds directly to the PX domains of SNX5/6 but not SNX1/2 and that IncE is sufficient to disrupt retromer-dependent trafficking of CI-MPR (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by previous work by the authors cited.

claim: IncE is sufficient to disrupt retromer-dependent trafficking of CI-MPR.
source: We recently discovered that C. trachomatis IncE binds directly to the PX domains of SNX5/6 but not SNX1/2 and that IncE is sufficient to disrupt retromer-dependent trafficking of CI-MPR (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by previous work by the authors cited.

claim: SNX-BAR proteins relocalize from endosomes to the inclusion membrane during C. trachomatis infection.
source: In addition, we and others found that SNX-BAR proteins relocalize from endosomes to the inclusion membrane during C. trachomatis infection and that depletion of SNX5/6 enhances C. trachomatis replication (Aeberhard et al., 2015; Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by previous work by the authors and others cited.

claim: Depletion of SNX5/6 enhances C. trachomatis replication.
source: In addition, we and others found that SNX-BAR proteins relocalize from endosomes to the inclusion membrane during C. trachomatis infection and that depletion of SNX5/6 enhances C. trachomatis replication (Aeberhard et al., 2015; Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by previous work by the authors and others cited.

claim: IncE binding to SNX5/6 redirects SNX1/2/5/6 away from their normal functional location and thereby limits the ability of retromer to control C. trachomatis infection.
source: Our findings suggest that IncE binding to SNX5/6 redirects SNX1/2/5/6 away from their normal functional location and thereby limits the ability of retromer to control C. trachomatis infection (Mirrashidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings cited.

claim: The crystal structure was solved by molecular replacement at a resolution of 2.31 Å, using the SNX5-PX apo-structure as a model (PDB ID 3HPC).
source: The crystal structure was solved by molecular replacement at a resolution of 2.31 Å, using the SNX5-PX apo-structure as a model (PDB ID 3HPC) ([Koharudin et al., 2009] and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the method used to solve the structure.

claim: The structure contained four copies of the SNX5-PX:IncE complex in the asymmetric unit, which are all less than 0.41 Å RMSD between the molecules.
source: The structure contained four copies of the SNX5-PX:IncE complex in the asymmetric unit, which are all less than 0.41 Å RMSD between the molecules and do not appear different in conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Amino acids 108–110 and 132 of IncE were disordered in the crystal and could not be built.
source: Using bulky hydrophobic residues as a guide, we were able to unambiguously place the IncE108-132 peptide into the density, although amino acids 108–110 and 132 were disordered in the crystal and could not be built.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The final model of the complex had Rwork/Rfree 20.32/26.00.
source: The final model of the complex (Rwork/Rfree 20.32/26.00) showed that IncE108-132 forms a β-hairpin that does not appear to be externally stabilized by its interaction with the PX domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a quality metric for the crystal structure.

claim: IncE108-132 forms a β-hairpin that does not appear to be externally stabilized by its interaction with the PX domain.
source: The final model of the complex (Rwork/Rfree 20.32/26.00) showed that IncE108-132 forms a β-hairpin that does not appear to be externally stabilized by its interaction with the PX domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IncE108-132 binds in a deep, hydrophobic groove that is approximately 10 Å x 18 Å in area running perpendicular to the long axis of the SNX5-PX domain.
source: When compared to the apo-SNX5-PX structure (PDB ID 3HPC [Koharudin et al., 2009]), IncE108-132 was found to bind in a deep, hydrophobic groove that is approximately 10 Å x 18 Å in area running perpendicular to the long axis of the SNX5-PX domain.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the bound and apo structures.

claim: SNX5-PX20-180 is a mixed α-β structure with three antiparallel β-sheets running along the surface of a long α-helix (α3) stabilized by two shorter helices.
source: SNX5-PX20-180 is a mixed α-β structure with three antiparallel β-sheets running along the surface of a long α-helix (α3) stabilized by two shorter helices.
evidence: This is a structural description from the crystal structure.

claim: Two of the helices extend past the end of the β-sheets to form a long α-helical hairpin not seen in the crystal structures of other SNX-PX domains.
source: Two of the helices extend past the end of the β-sheets to form a long α-helical hairpin not seen in the crystal structures of other SNX-PX domains (Koharudin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a structural observation comparing SNX5-PX to other SNX-PX domains, supported by citation.

claim: In the SNX5-PX20-180:IncE108-132 structure, the SNX5-PX20-180 β-sheet is completed by the IncE108-132 β-hairpin, which binds on the surface of the α-helical hairpin in the hydrophobic groove, hydrogen bonding with the SNX5-PX20-180 β-sheet to form a hybrid, five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet.
source: In the SNX5-PX20-180:IncE108-132 structure, the SNX5-PX20-180 β-sheet is completed by the IncE108-132 β-hairpin, which binds on the surface of the α-helical hairpin in the hydrophobic groove, hydrogen bonding with the SNX5-PX20-180 β-sheet to form a hybrid, five-stranded antiparallel β-sheet (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Outside of β-sheet formation, the structure of SNX5 complexed with IncE108-132 is notable for its almost complete lack of hydrogen bonding or ionic charge-charge interactions.
source: Outside of this β-sheet formation, the structure of SNX5 complexed with IncE108-132 is notable for its almost complete lack of hydrogen bonding or ionic charge-charge interactions (Figure 1B), relying instead on the formation of a small hydrophobic core at the interface of the two proteins.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The SNX5-PX:IncE interface relies on the formation of a small hydrophobic core at the interface of the two proteins.
source: Outside of this β-sheet formation, the structure of SNX5 complexed with IncE108-132 is notable for its almost complete lack of hydrogen bonding or ionic charge-charge interactions (Figure 1B), relying instead on the formation of a small hydrophobic core at the interface of the two proteins.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The hydrophobic core at the SNX5-PX:IncE interface buries five residues: Y132, L133 and F136 from SNX5-PX20-180 and V114 and F116 from IncE108-132.
source: This core buries five residues at the interface: Y132, L133 and F136 from SNX5-PX20-180 and V114 and F116 from IncE108-132 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SNX5 PIP binding site binds specifically to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), although the binding is weak.
source: For example, the SNX5 PIP binding site binds specifically to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), although the binding is weak (Koharudin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the SNX5-PX20-180:IncE108-132 crystal structure, there is no direct interaction between IncE108-132 and the previously observed PIP binding pocket.
source: In the SNX5-PX20-180:IncE108-132 crystal structure, we observed no direct interaction between IncE108-132 and the previously observed PIP binding pocket (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The changes between the apo-SNX5-PX structure and the IncE108-132 bound SNX5-PX20-180 structure are small and consist mainly of an inward rotation of the SNX5 α-helical hairpin ~30° toward the IncE peptide.
source: The changes between the apo-SNX5-PX structure and the IncE108-132 bound SNX5-PX20-180 structure are small and consist mainly of an inward rotation of the SNX5 α-helical hairpin ~30° toward the IncE peptide.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the apo and bound structures.

claim: The SNX5 α-helical hairpin region appears to be quite flexible as it has the highest B-factors in both the apo- and IncE-bound structures.
source: This region appears to be quite flexible as it has the highest B-factors in both the apo- and IncE-bound structures (Koharudin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by citation.

claim: IncE108-132 does not compete with binding of SNX5 to lipid head groups.
source: IncE108-132 did not compete with binding of SNX5 to lipid head groups nor did it affect the pattern of PIPs engaged by SNX5-PX20-180 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipid binding assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: IncE108-132 does not affect the pattern of PIPs engaged by SNX5-PX20-180.
source: IncE108-132 did not compete with binding of SNX5 to lipid head groups nor did it affect the pattern of PIPs engaged by SNX5-PX20-180 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lipid binding assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Binding of IncE to SNX5-PX does not interfere with SNX5 binding to PIPs.
source: Together, this data supports the notion that binding of IncE to SNX5-PX does not interfere with SNX5 binding to PIPs.
evidence: This is concluded from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: IncE108-132 does not bind at the BAR domain interface of SNX5.
source: IncE108-132 does not bind at this BAR domain interface, and the BAR domain interface does not appear to be significantly altered by binding of IncE.
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The BAR domain interface does not appear to be significantly altered by binding of IncE.
source: IncE108-132 does not bind at this BAR domain interface, and the BAR domain interface does not appear to be significantly altered by binding of IncE.
evidence: This is inferred from structural modeling.

claim: The interaction between SNX5 and SNX1 through their respective BAR domains would not be affected by interaction of SNX5 with IncE.
source: We conclude that the interaction between SNX5 and SNX1 through their respective BAR domains would not be affected by interaction of SNX5 with IncE.
evidence: This is concluded from structural analysis and modeling.

claim: The three residues buried at the IncE108-132 interface (Y132, L133, F136) are identical in all species of metazoans for which sequence data is available.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of 763 unique sequences of SNX5, SNX6, and SNX32 allowed comparison of the IncE binding surface of each species and revealed that the three residues buried at the IncE108-132 interface are identical in all species of metazoans for which sequence data is available (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: This conservation was observed even in the most distantly related sequence analyzed, SNX6 from Trichinella spiralis, which shows overall identity of only 49%.
source: This conservation was observed even in the most distantly related sequence we analyzed, SNX6 from Trichinella spiralis, which shows overall identity of only 49%.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The region of conservation in the SNX5/6/32 family extends outside of the hydrophobic groove that binds to IncE and includes several solvent exposed residues, including K138.
source: This region of conservation in the SNX5/6/32 family extends outside of the hydrophobic groove that binds to IncE and includes several solvent exposed residues, including K138 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis and structural mapping shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The conserved residues in the SNX5 hydrophobic groove are absent in other SNX-BAR proteins including SNX1 and SNX2.
source: Importantly, these residues are absent in other SNX-BAR proteins including SNX1 and SNX2, as has been previously noted (Koharudin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison and citation.

claim: The residues lining the SNX5 hydrophobic groove are not involved in the core folding of the SNX5/6/32-PX domain.
source: Thus, the residues lining the SNX5 hydrophobic groove are not involved in the core folding of the SNX5/6/32-PX domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and conservation pattern.

claim: The residues lining the SNX5 hydrophobic groove are solvent exposed in the unbound crystal structure.
source: These residues are solvent exposed in the unbound crystal structure (Koharudin et al., 2009), and yet they are identical throughout metazoan evolution, implying an essential function.
evidence: This is supported by the apo structure cited.

claim: The IncE binding surface on SNX5 is highly conserved throughout metazoan evolution, implying an essential function.
source: These residues are solvent exposed in the unbound crystal structure (Koharudin et al., 2009), and yet they are identical throughout metazoan evolution, implying an essential function.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation analysis.

claim: The IncE binding surface on SNX5 likely serves a normal physiological role by mediating an interaction with another macromolecule.
source: Together, our finding that the IncE binding surface is highly conserved in the SNX5/6/32 family of proteins suggests that it serves a normal physiological role, most likely by mediating an interaction with another macromolecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation analysis.

claim: Disruption of the small hydrophobic core at the SNX5-PX20-180:IncE108-132 interface would destabilize the complex.
source: The crystal structure predicts that disruption of the small hydrophobic core at the SNX5-PX20-180:IncE108-132 interface would destabilize the complex.
evidence: This is predicted from the structural analysis.

claim: SNX5Y132:IncEV114 and SNX5F136:IncEF116 form stable van der Waals and π-π stacking interactions that appear to be central to the specificity of the interaction.
source: In particular, SNX5Y132:IncEV114 and SNX5F136:IncEF116 form stable van der Waals and π-π stacking interactions that appear to be central to the specificity of the interaction.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of IncE101-132 with SNX5 is dependent upon Y132 or F136.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation of IncE101-132 with SNX5 was dependent upon Y132 or F136, confirming the importance of these aromatic amino acid contacts in the formation of the SNX5:IncE complex (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FLAG-SNX5Y132D,F136D fails to localize to the C. trachomatis inclusion.
source: FLAG-SNX5Y132D,F136D fails to localize to the inclusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although endogenous SNX6 was still recruited.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous SNX6 is still recruited to the C. trachomatis inclusion when FLAG-SNX5Y132D,F136D is expressed.
source: FLAG-SNX5Y132D,F136D fails to localize to the inclusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although endogenous SNX6 was still recruited.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: IncE interacts with the SNX5 hydrophobic binding groove.
source: Together, these data provide further support that IncE interacts with the SNX5 hydrophobic binding groove.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis and localization data.

claim: IncE is likely disrupting an interaction between SNX5 and a previously unappreciated host cell protein through a shared binding surface.
source: Given the high conservation of the IncE binding surface, we reasoned that IncE is likely disrupting an interaction between SNX5 and a previously unappreciated host cell protein through a shared binding surface.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the conservation analysis.

claim: Mutating the SNX5 hydrophobic groove would lead to loss of the native interaction with a host protein.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that mutating this surface would lead to loss of the native interaction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that motivated the AP-MS experiment.

claim: Six proteins were found to significantly interact with SNX5WT protein according to the SAINT algorithm.
source: Although six proteins were found to significantly interact with SNX5WT protein according to the SAINT algorithm, only two proteins, CI-MPR and Insulin-like Growth Factor I (IGF1R), bound differentially to SNX5WT and the SNX5 hydrophobic groove mutants, as evidenced by significantly different SAINT scores (Table 1, Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the AP-MS data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Only two proteins, CI-MPR and Insulin-like Growth Factor I (IGF1R), bound differentially to SNX5WT and the SNX5 hydrophobic groove mutants.
source: Although six proteins were found to significantly interact with SNX5WT protein according to the SAINT algorithm, only two proteins, CI-MPR and Insulin-like Growth Factor I (IGF1R), bound differentially to SNX5WT and the SNX5 hydrophobic groove mutants, as evidenced by significantly different SAINT scores (Table 1, Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the AP-MS data shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: SNX1 co-affinity purified with both WT and mutant SNX5.
source: Importantly, SNX1 co-affinity purified with both WT and mutant SNX5 (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3), consistent with the notion that disrupting the IncE binding surface does not cause major alterations to the SNX5 structure.
evidence: This is supported by the AP-MS data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Disrupting the IncE binding surface does not cause major alterations to the SNX5 structure.
